symptom: a bloated belly that came and went for years
hook: a giant balloon of gas was living in the lower belly
whatYouSee: A huge smooth round balloon of gas with a thin wall sits in the left lower abdomen and pushes the bowel aside.
whyItMatters: A giant sigmoid diverticulum is a rare complication of diverticular disease. A one-way valve lets gas into the pouch but not out so it inflates over time. It can mimic sigmoid volvulus and may perforate or twist.
treatment: Treatment is usually surgical resection of the diverticulum with the involved sigmoid colon. This removes the risk of perforation and volvulus.
takeaway: A giant smooth gas balloon without haustra beside the sigmoid colon is a giant sigmoid diverticulum.

findings: Frontal (AP) supine-appearing abdominal radiograph covering the lower chest to the pelvis
Markedly dilated, thin-walled, gas-filled round loop in the left mid and lower abdomen, roughly 12-13 cm, with a smooth sharp wall
The large loop has a single rounded lumen with no haustral folds or internal septations visible

A column of haustrated gas-filled colon curves around the left and upper margin of the large loop, consistent with the descending and sigmoid colon, with the colon mildly gas-distended along the left flank
Multiple gas-filled small bowel and right-sided bowel loops in the right abdomen, with mild to moderate gas distension and valvulae or haustral markings
Gas bubble in the left upper quadrant consistent with the gastric fundus
No obvious free intraperitoneal air, pneumatosis or portal venous gas seen
Lumbar spine and pelvis appear intact with no definite fracture
Lateral left-sided dark band and a vertical straight edge in the upper left of the image are likely collimation or detector edge artifacts
differential: Sigmoid volvulus with a markedly distended closed-loop sigmoid colon (coffee-bean or omega-type loop) causing large bowel obstruction
Distal large bowel obstruction from another cause (e.g. stricture or mass) with a dilated sigmoid colon
Megacolon or megasigmoid, chronic or functional, without torsion
anatomyConcerns: The vertical straight edge and black lateral band are acquisition or collimation artifacts rather than pathology
Rotation and projection are slightly asymmetric, and the upper image is cropped, so the diaphragm and lung bases are not fully assessed
Supine versus erect position cannot be confirmed, as no air-fluid levels are clearly shown
